cse-1998-b-68.approach: Encode the states in binary (Q2Q1Q0), write the present-state/next-state table, treat the four unused states as don't-cares and read each D input directly from the table (D flip-flops: D = next state).

steps.title: Minimise each D
steps.body:
- $D_2 = 1$ only for 001; with don't-care 101: $D_2 = \overline{Q_1}\,Q_0$ (100 gives 0, 010/011 give 0).
- $D_1 = 1$ for 100 and 010, $0$ for 001 and 011: $D_1 = \overline{Q_0}$.
- $D_0 = 1$ for 010 and 011, $0$ for 001 and 100: $D_0 = Q_1$.

steps.title: Circuit
steps.body: Three D flip-flops on a common clock: $D_2 = \overline{Q_1}Q_0$ (one AND gate with $\overline{Q_1}$), $D_1 = \overline{Q_0}$, $D_0 = Q_1$. Initialise to 001 (preset $Q_0$).

steps.title: Self-starting check
steps.body: Unused states: $000 \to 010$, $101 \to 100$, $110 \to 011$, $111 \to 001$ — every one enters the main cycle $1\to4\to2\to3$ in one clock, so the counter is self-starting.

answer.value: D flip-flops (Q2Q1Q0): D2 = Q̄1·Q0, D1 = Q̄0, D0 = Q1 (001→100→010→011→001; self-starting)

pitfalls: Mixing the bit order of the state code between the table and the equations.
Not checking unused states — a counter can lock up in an unused loop.
cse-1998-b-68.verification: Applied the equations to each used state: 001 gives D2 = 1, D1 = 0, D0 = 0 → 100 ✓; 100 → 010 ✓; 010 → 011 ✓; 011 → 001 ✓.

animation.caption: * = forced by the chosen equations (don't-care rows)

cse-1998-b-69.approach: Work out which tracks/sides the 35 sectors occupy, then add initial rotational latency, the reading time (25 ms per sector at 300 RPM) and the track-to-track steps. The question leaves several assumptions open, so state them.
cse-1998-b-69.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Sectors / track | 8 |
| Sides | 2 |
| Speed | 300 RPM |
| Step time | 8 ms |
| Start | track 10, sector 3 (head already on track 10) |

steps.title: Rotation figures
steps.body: $300$ RPM $\Rightarrow$ one revolution $= 60/300 = 0.2\,s = 200$ ms; one sector $= 200/8 = 25$ ms.

steps.title: Where the 35 sectors are
steps.body: Sectors 3–8 of track 10, side 0: $6$; track 10, side 1: $8$ (total $14$); track 11, both sides: $16$ (total $30$); track 12, side 0: $5$ (total $35$). Switching sides is electronic (no seek), so only **2 steps** are needed ($10\to11$, $11\to12$).

steps.title: Add up (assumptions stated)
steps.body:
Assume: average initial latency of half a revolution $=100$ ms; the 1-sector buffer is emptied during the inter-sector gap, so consecutive sectors are read back-to-back; tracks are skewed so the first sector of the next track arrives just after the 8 ms step.

$$T = 100 + 35\times 25 + 2\times 8 = 100 + 875 + 16 = 991\text{ ms}$$

steps.title: Without track skew
steps.body:
If sector 1 of the new track is aligned with sector 1 of the old one, it has already passed when the 8 ms step completes, so each step costs a full revolution (200 ms):

$$T = 100 + 875 + 2\times 200 = 1375\text{ ms}$$

answer.value: ≈ 991 ms: 100 ms average initial rotational latency + 35 × 25 ms = 875 ms of reading + 2 track steps × 8 ms = 16 ms (sectors: 6 on track 10 side 0, 8 on track 10 side 1, 16 on track 11, 5 on track 12). If sector 1 of the next track is not skewed, each step costs a full revolution instead: 100 + 875 + 2 × 200 = 1375 ms.

pitfalls: Forgetting the second side: a cylinder (track 10) holds 16 sectors, not 8.
Answers of a few tens of ms are impossible — 35 sectors need at least 35 × 25 = 875 ms of reading alone.
cse-1998-b-69.verification: 6 + 8 + 16 + 5 = 35 sectors; lower bound 875 ms confirms the order of magnitude.

cse-1998-b-70.approach: Map the loop's n = km consecutive blocks onto the l sets (block i → set i mod l) and check whether every set can hold its share; if yes only the first pass misses. For l = 1 the loop exceeds the k-block cache and a cyclic access pattern defeats LRU/FIFO.

steps.title: Does the loop fit?
steps.body: Cache capacity $= l$ sets $\times k$ blocks $= kl$ blocks. Loop size $= n = km$ blocks with $m \le l$, so $km \le kl$. Consecutive blocks spread over the sets cyclically, so each set receives at most $\lceil km/l \rceil \le k$ blocks — every set can hold all of its loop blocks.

steps.title: Hit ratio for 1 < m ≤ l
steps.body:
Pass 1: each of the $n$ blocks misses once (compulsory). Passes 2–100: all hits.

$$h = \frac{100n - n}{100n} = \frac{99}{100} = 0.99$$

Counting individual word references ($b$ words per block): $h = 1 - \dfrac{n}{100\,n\,b} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{100b}$.

Average access time $t_{avg} = h\,t_c + (1-h)\,t_m$.

steps.title: Case l = 1
steps.body: One set of $k$ blocks (fully associative), but the loop has $mk > k$ blocks (since $m > 1$). With LRU (or FIFO) and a cyclic reference string longer than the cache, the block needed next is always the one just evicted, so **every block reference misses**: $h = 0$ (per word only the spatial-locality hits remain: $h = 1 - 1/b$).

answer.value: The loop (n = km blocks ≤ kl blocks) fits in the cache: only the first pass misses, so h = (100n − n)/(100n) = 0.99 per block reference (1 − 1/(100b) per word). For l = 1 the cache holds only k blocks but the loop has mk > k blocks, so with LRU/FIFO every block reference misses: h = 0 (1 − 1/b per word, from spatial locality only).

pitfalls: Assuming a set-associative cache can conflict even though each set receives at most k loop blocks.
Applying the 1 < m ≤ l formula to l = 1, where that range is empty and the loop no longer fits.
cse-1998-b-70.verification: Example: k = 2, l = 4, m = 3 → 6 blocks over 4 sets (2,2,1,1 per set ≤ 2) → 6 misses in 600 references → 0.99. With l = 1, k = 2, 4 blocks A B C D cycling under LRU: every access misses.

cse-1998-b-72.approach: Last postorder element is the root; split the inorder sequence around it and recurse on each side with the matching postorder segment.

steps.title: Root
steps.body: Postorder ends with **b** → root $= b$. Inorder `a f | b | c d g e`: left $\{a,f\}$, right $\{c,d,g,e\}$. Postorder splits the same way: `a f | c g e d | b`.

steps.title: Left subtree
steps.body: Postorder `a f` → root **f**; inorder `a f` → a is f's left child.

steps.title: Right subtree
steps.body: Postorder `c g e d` → root **d**; inorder `c | d | g e` → left child c, right part $\{g,e\}$ with postorder `g e` → root **e**, inorder `g e` → g is e's left child.

answer.value: Root b; left subtree f with left child a; right subtree d with left child c and right child e, where e has left child g

pitfalls: Using the first postorder element as root (that is preorder's rule).
cse-1998-b-72.verification: Inorder of the built tree: a f b c d g e ✓; postorder: a f c g e d b ✓.

cse-1998-b-75.approach: Synthesise for each L both its integer value and its length; the fractional part is L2.val / 2^{L2.len}.

steps.title: Attributes
steps.body: `L.val` (value of the bit string as an integer), `L.len` (number of bits), `B.val`, `S.val` — all synthesized.

steps.title: Translation scheme
steps.body:
| Production | Semantic rule |
|---|---|
| $S \to L_1 . L_2$ | $S.val = L_1.val + L_2.val / 2^{L_2.len}$ |
| $S \to L$ | $S.val = L.val$ |
| $L \to L_1 B$ | $L.val = 2 L_1.val + B.val$; $L.len = L_1.len + 1$ |
| $L \to B$ | $L.val = B.val$; $L.len = 1$ |
| $B \to 0$ | $B.val = 0$ |
| $B \to 1$ | $B.val = 1$ |

answer.value: S→L1.L2 {S.val = L1.val + L2.val/2^{L2.len}}; S→L {S.val = L.val}; L→L1B {L.val = 2L1.val + B.val; L.len = L1.len + 1}; L→B {L.val = B.val; L.len = 1}; B→0 {B.val = 0}; B→1 {B.val = 1}

pitfalls: Using an inherited position/weight attribute for the fraction — the question demands synthesized attributes only, hence the length attribute.

cse-1998-b-79.approach: Find courses having at least one prerequisite the student has NOT completed, and subtract them from all courses (division via set difference).

steps.title: Courses done by 2310
steps.body: $T \leftarrow \rho_{T(\text{pre-Cno})}\big(\pi_{Cno}(\sigma_{\text{student no}=2310}(\text{COMPLETED}))\big)$

steps.title: Missing prerequisites
steps.body: $\text{PRE-REQ} - (\pi_{Cno}(\text{PRE-REQ}) \times T)$ keeps exactly the pairs (Cno, pre-Cno) whose pre-Cno is not in $T$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body:
$$\pi_{Cno}(\text{COURSES}) - \pi_{Cno}\big(\text{PRE-REQ} - (\pi_{Cno}(\text{PRE-REQ}) \times T)\big)$$

Courses with no prerequisites are included (vacuously all completed).

answer.value: T ← ρ_{pre-Cno}(π_Cno(σ_{student no=2310}(COMPLETED))); result = π_Cno(COURSES) − π_Cno(PRE-REQ − (π_Cno(PRE-REQ) × T))

cse-1998-b-79.shortcut: Equivalently π_Cno(COURSES) − π_Cno(PRE-REQ ▷ T) (anti-join on pre-Cno).
pitfalls: Using PRE-REQ ÷ T — that returns courses whose prerequisites include ALL of the student's completed courses, the reverse condition.
cse-1998-b-79.verification: Example: PRE-REQ = {(C3,C1),(C3,C2),(C4,C1)}, T = {C1}: missing pairs = {(C3,C2)} → result = all courses except C3 ✓.

cse-1998-b-67-a.approach: Feed the TTL pulse to a single input line the 8085 can sample in software — the SID pin (read with RIM) or one bit of an 8155/8255 port — and time it by counting a fixed-length polling loop (or gate an 8155/8253 timer with it).

steps.title: Minimum system
steps.body:
- **8085 CPU** with a crystal (e.g. 6 MHz → 3 MHz clock, $T = 0.333\,\mu s$).
- Address latch **74LS373** on $AD_0$–$AD_7$ driven by **ALE** to demultiplex the low address byte.
- **EPROM 2732/2764** for the program, **RAM 6116** (or an 8155, which gives 256 B RAM + ports + a 14-bit timer) for the count.
- Address decoder (**74LS138**) on $A_{15}$–$A_{11}$ produces the chip selects; $\overline{RD}$, $\overline{WR}$, $IO/\overline{M}$ give the read/write strobes.

steps.title: Connecting the pulse
steps.body:
The source is TTL compatible, so no level shifting is needed. Connect the pulse (through a 74LS14 Schmitt buffer for clean edges) to

- the **SID** pin (pin 5) — read by `RIM` into bit $D_7$ of A, **or**
- one input bit (say $PA_0$) of an **8155/8255** port configured as input.

Optionally connect it also to the **GATE** of an 8155/8253 counter so the hardware counts clock pulses only while the pulse is HIGH.

steps.title: Display / output
steps.body: The measured count (pulse width $= \text{count} \times \text{loop time}$) is stored in RAM or sent to an output port / seven-segment display driven by the second port of the 8155/8255.

answer.value: 8085 + latch + EPROM/RAM (or 8155) + decoder; TTL pulse wired to SID (read with RIM) or to an input bit of an 8155/8255 port (optionally to a timer GATE); width = loop count × loop time

cse-1998-b-67-a.shortcut: SID needs no extra chip: one wire plus RIM is the cheapest pulse input on the 8085.
pitfalls: Forgetting the address latch (ALE) needed to demultiplex AD0–AD7.
Starting the count in the middle of a pulse — the software must first wait for a rising edge.
cse-1998-b-67-a.verification: Checked that every block of the schematic (clock, demultiplexing, memory, decoding, input line) is required for the program in part (b) to run.

cse-1998-b-67-b.approach: Poll the input bit: wait for LOW (so we do not start inside a pulse), wait for the rising edge, then increment a 16-bit counter in a loop of known T-states until the line falls. Width = count × loop T-states × clock period.

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body:
- Pulse on **SID**; `RIM` copies it into bit $D_7$ of A.
- 3 MHz clock ($T = 0.333\,\mu s$), no interrupts during measurement.
- Pulse shorter than $65535$ loop passes (16-bit counter in HL).
- Result stored at 2050H–2051H.

steps.title: Program
steps.body:
```asm
        LXI  H,0000H   ; HL = counter
WAITL:  RIM            ; A7 = SID
        ANI  80H
        JNZ  WAITL     ; wait while HIGH (skip a pulse already in progress)
WAITH:  RIM
        ANI  80H
        JZ   WAITH     ; wait for the rising edge
COUNT:  INX  H         ; 6 T
        RIM            ; 4 T
        ANI  80H       ; 7 T
        JNZ  COUNT     ; 10 T (taken) - loop while HIGH
        SHLD 2050H     ; save count
        HLT
```

steps.title: Converting the count
steps.body:
One pass of the `COUNT` loop takes $6+4+7+10 = 27$ T-states $= 27 \times 0.333\,\mu s = 9\,\mu s$.

$$\text{Width} \approx \text{count} \times 9\,\mu s$$

Resolution is $9\,\mu s$; the maximum measurable width is $65535 \times 9\,\mu s \approx 0.59\,s$.

answer.value: Wait for LOW, wait for rising edge, then loop {INX H; RIM; ANI 80H; JNZ} until the line goes LOW; width = count × 27 T-states (9 µs at 3 MHz)

pitfalls: INX H does not affect flags, so overflow of HL must be bounded by an assumption (or checked separately).
Using the T-states of the not-taken JNZ (7) for the loop — the loop repeats on the taken branch (10).
cse-1998-b-67-b.verification: 8085 T-states: INX rp = 6, RIM = 4, ANI = 7, JNZ taken = 10 → 27 per pass; 27 × 1/3 µs = 9 µs.

animation.code:
LXI  H,0000H
WAITL: RIM
ANI  80H
JNZ  WAITL
WAITH: RIM
ANI  80H
JZ   WAITH
COUNT: INX  H
RIM
ANI  80H
JNZ  COUNT
SHLD 2050H
HLT

cse-1998-b-71-a.approach: Trace the four assignments on a concrete list p → X → Y → Z.

steps.title: Name the nodes
steps.body: Let p point to node P with $P \to X \to Y \to Z$.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body:
1. `q := p->next` → $q = X$.
2. `p->next := q->next` → $P \to Y$.
3. `q->next := (q->next)->next` → $X$'s next was $Y$, so $X \to Z$.
4. `(p->next)->next := q` → $Y \to X$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: List is now $P \to Y \to X \to Z$: the **two nodes following p are swapped** (by relinking, not by copying data).

answer.value: Swaps the two nodes that follow p (p→X→Y→Z becomes p→Y→X→Z)

pitfalls: Step 3 uses q->next before it is overwritten — it reads the old link X → Y.
cse-1998-b-71-a.verification: Walk from P after the trace: P → Y → X → Z, every node reached exactly once, no cycle.

cse-1998-b-71-b.approach: Use precedence: function application binds tightest, then * and /, then −; left-to-right for equal precedence.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Postfix: `3 x 1 + log * a 2 / -`

pitfalls: Placing log before its argument (prefix style) — in postfix the unary operator follows its operand.
cse-1998-b-71-b.verification: Evaluating the postfix with a stack: push 3, x, 1; + → x+1; log → log(x+1); * → 3·log(x+1); push a, 2; / → a/2; − → original expression.

cse-1998-b-73-a.approach: The sparsest AVL tree of height h has one subtree of height h−1 and the other of height h−2 (the most unbalanced allowed), each itself minimal.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Root + minimal AVL tree of height $h-1$ + minimal AVL tree of height $h-2$ (heights may differ by at most 1).

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body:
Height = edges on the longest root–leaf path (single node has height 0):

$$N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1,\quad N(0) = 1,\ N(1) = 2$$

This gives $N(h) = F_{h+3} - 1$ (Fibonacci).

pitfalls: If height counts levels (single node = height 1) the base cases shift to N(1) = 1, N(2) = 2.
cse-1998-b-73-a.verification: N(2) = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4: root, a 2-node child and a leaf — the smallest AVL tree of height 2.

cse-1998-b-73-b.approach: Unroll N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 from N(0) = 1, N(1) = 2.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Smallest AVL tree of height 8 has **88** nodes (height in edges). With height counted in levels it would be $N(8) = 54$.

pitfalls: Mixing the two height conventions — check N(0)/N(1) before iterating.

cse-1998-b-74-a.approach: One mandatory letter followed by 0 to 5 letters or digits.

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Let $L = (a+b+\dots+z+A+\dots+Z)$, $D = (0+1+\dots+9)$. First character: $L$. Remaining $0$–$5$ characters, each $L$ or $D$: $(L+D+\epsilon)^5$.

steps.title: Expression
steps.body: $$L\,(L+D+\epsilon)^5 \;=\; L\big(\epsilon + (L+D) + (L+D)^2 + \dots + (L+D)^5\big)$$

pitfalls: Writing L(L+D)* — that allows identifiers longer than six characters.
cse-1998-b-74-a.verification: Lengths produced: 1 (all ε) up to 6 (no ε) — exactly "up to six", first symbol always a letter.

cse-1998-b-74-b.approach: Compute FIRST of each right-hand side and FOLLOW for the ε-producing Y; place A → α under FIRST(α), and Y → ε under FOLLOW(Y).

steps.title: FIRST and FOLLOW
steps.body:
| Non-terminal | FIRST | FOLLOW |
|---|---|---|
| Program | begin | \$ |
| X | d, s | end |
| Y | semi, ε | end |

FOLLOW(X) = {end} (from Program), FOLLOW(Y) = FOLLOW(X) = {end} (Y ends X → sY).

steps.title: Table
steps.body:
| | begin | d | s | semi | end |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Program | Program → begin d semi X end | | | | |
| X | | X → d semi X | X → sY | | |
| Y | | | | Y → semi s Y | Y → ε |

No cell has two entries, confirming the grammar is LL(1).

answer.value: M[Program, begin] = Program → begin d semi X end; M[X, d] = X → d semi X; M[X, s] = X → sY; M[Y, semi] = Y → semi s Y; M[Y, end] = Y → ε

pitfalls: Putting Y → ε under semi — it goes under FOLLOW(Y) = {end}.
cse-1998-b-74-b.verification: Parsed "begin d semi s semi s end": Program → begin d semi X end; X → sY; Y → semi s Y; Y → ε on end ✓.

cse-1998-b-76-a.approach: Average response (turnaround) time is minimised by Shortest Job First; place x according to its size.

steps.title: Why SJF
steps.body: With jobs run back-to-back, the $i$-th job's completion adds its run time to every later job, so the total is $\sum (n-i+1)\,t_i$; it is minimised by running the shortest job first (exchange argument).

pitfalls: Giving one fixed order — the position of x depends on its value.
cse-1998-b-76-a.verification: Swapping any adjacent pair with the longer job first increases the total by (longer − shorter) > 0.

cse-1998-b-76-b.approach: Read the graph: after S1, two independent branches run concurrently — S3 alone and the chain S2 → S4 — and S5 waits for both. The direct edges S1→S4 and S1→S5 are implied by the others.

steps.title: Dependencies
steps.body: Edges: $S_1\to S_2, S_1\to S_3, S_1\to S_4, S_1\to S_5, S_2\to S_4, S_3\to S_5, S_4\to S_5$. $S_1\to S_4$ follows from $S_1\to S_2\to S_4$ and $S_1\to S_5$ from $S_1\to S_3\to S_5$, so they need no extra code.

steps.title: Program

answer.value: S1; parbegin S3; begin S2; S4 end parend; S5

pitfalls: Putting S2, S3 and S4 all in one parbegin — S4 must wait for S2.
cse-1998-b-76-b.verification: Every edge is respected: S1 precedes the parbegin, S2 precedes S4 inside the sequential block, and S5 starts only after parend (both S3 and S4 done).

cse-1998-b-77-a.approach: Compare the sizes: a free list stores one D-bit address per free block; a bit map stores one bit per block.

steps.title: Sizes
steps.body: Free list: $F \cdot D$ bits. Bit map: one bit per block $= 13$ bits (in general $B$ bits for $B$ blocks).

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: Free list is smaller when $F\cdot D < 13$ (generally $F \cdot D < B$, i.e. $F/B < 1/D$).

answer.value: F·D < 13 (in general F·D < B for B blocks)

pitfalls: Comparing with the number of free blocks instead of the total number of blocks for the bit map.
cse-1998-b-77-a.verification: With D = 16 and B = 13 the free list wins only when F = 0 — consistent with bit maps being preferred on small disks.

cse-1998-b-77-b.approach: Since a record is exactly one sector, convert the start address to a linear sector number, add n, and convert back with division and remainders.

steps.title: Linearise the start
steps.body: Number cylinders, tracks and sectors from 0. Sectors per cylinder $= t\cdot s$. Start: $N_0 = (c_L\, t + t_L)\, s + s_L$.

steps.title: Record n
steps.body: With $r_l = s_l$, record $n$ (first record $n=0$) occupies sector $N = N_0 + n$.

steps.title: Back to CHS
steps.body:
$$\text{cylinder} = \left\lfloor \frac{N}{t\,s} \right\rfloor,\quad \text{track} = \left\lfloor \frac{N \bmod (t\,s)}{s} \right\rfloor,\quad \text{sector} = N \bmod s$$

(If records are numbered from 1, use $n-1$; if sectors are numbered from 1, add 1 to the sector.)

answer.value: With N = (c_L·t + t_L)·s + s_L + n (records numbered from 0): cylinder = ⌊N/(t·s)⌋, track = ⌊(N mod t·s)/s⌋, sector = N mod s

pitfalls: Forgetting that a contiguous file wraps from the last sector of a track to the next track and then the next cylinder.
cse-1998-b-77-b.verification: t = 2, s = 4, start (0,1,3), n = 1: N = (0+1)·4 + 3 + 1 = 8 → cylinder 1, track 0, sector 0 — the sector right after (0,1,3) ✓.

cse-1998-b-78-a.approach: List the FDs implied by the meaning, then test 2NF (partial dependency) and 3NF (transitive dependency).

steps.title: FDs
steps.body: Book-id → Subject-Category, Name-of-Author; Name-of-Author → Nationality-of-Author.

steps.title: Test
steps.body: Key is the single attribute Book-id, so no partial dependency → **2NF**. But Book-id → Name-of-Author → Nationality-of-Author is transitive (Nationality is non-prime and Author is not a superkey) → not 3NF.

pitfalls: Calling it 3NF because the key is a single attribute — that only guarantees 2NF.
cse-1998-b-78-a.verification: Decomposing into (Book-id, Subject, Author) and (Author, Nationality) removes the transitive dependency, confirming 3NF was violated.

cse-1998-b-78-b.approach: With the composite key (Name-of-Author, Book-title), attributes depending on Name-of-Author alone are partial dependencies.

steps.title: FDs
steps.body: Name-of-Author → Nationality-of-Author, Author-address (author facts); (Name-of-Author, Book-title) → Book-id, Subject-Category.

steps.title: Test
steps.body: Nationality and Author-address are non-prime and depend on **part** of the key (Name-of-Author) → partial dependency → not 2NF. Attributes are atomic → **1NF**.

pitfalls: Overlooking that Name-of-Author is only part of the new key.
cse-1998-b-78-b.verification: Any non-prime attribute determined by a proper subset of a candidate key violates 2NF — Nationality is such an attribute.
